Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph from the early 1960s shows demonstrators participating in a sit-in at a segregated lunch counter in the American South. Civil rights activists — Black and some white — are seated at the counter while onlookers and counter staff are visible. The demonstrators sit calmly and are dressed neatly, practicing the nonviolent direct action strategy taught by civil rights organizations to challenge racial segregation in public accommodations.

(Photograph, c. 1960. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.)

Which form of protest is shown in this photograph?

choices.text: A sit-in, in which protesters occupied seats at a segregated facility and refused to leave
A boycott, in which protesters refused to purchase goods or services from segregated businesses
A voter registration drive, in which activists helped Black citizens register to vote at a public location
A march, in which protesters moved through public streets to demonstrate opposition to segregation laws

items.explanation: The photograph shows a sit-in — a form of nonviolent direct action in which protesters occupy seats at segregated facilities and refuse to leave. Sit-ins were used extensively during the Civil Rights Movement beginning with the Greensboro, North Carolina sit-ins in February 1960, rapidly spreading across the South. The strategy deliberately invited confrontation while maintaining nonviolent discipline, exposing the violence of segregation. Choice B describes a different form of protest. Choice C describes voter registration drives, not this action. Choice D describes street demonstrations, not counter occupations.

Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph from the early 1960s shows demonstrators participating in a sit-in at a segregated lunch counter in the American South. Civil rights activists — Black and some white — are seated at the counter while onlookers and counter staff are visible. The demonstrators sit calmly and are dressed neatly, practicing the nonviolent direct action strategy taught by civil rights organizations to challenge racial segregation in public accommodations.

(Photograph, c. 1960. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.)

How did sit-in protests at segregated lunch counters challenge segregation laws in the South?

choices.text: Sit-ins were fully legal under existing law, so they allowed activists to challenge segregation without risking arrest or confrontation
Sit-ins were deliberately conducted in secret to avoid media coverage and prevent violent reactions from segregationists

By occupying segregated facilities peacefully, sit-ins imposed economic costs on businesses, exposed the violence of segregation enforcement, and generated national sympathy for civil rights activists
Sit-ins worked by filing legal briefs in federal courts that directly challenged the constitutionality of segregation statutes

items.explanation: Sit-ins worked on multiple levels: they directly disrupted the business operations of segregated establishments, imposing economic costs on owners; they forced police and business owners into a dilemma — either serve Black customers or forcibly remove peacefully seated, well-dressed demonstrators, which made segregationists appear to be the aggressors; and television coverage exposed the brutality of segregation enforcement to national and international audiences, generating sympathy and support for the civil rights cause. Choice A is incorrect — sit-ins were illegal under local segregation ordinances and participants were often arrested. Choice B is backwards — sit-ins were designed to attract attention, not avoid it. Choice D misidentifies the mechanism.

Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph from the early 1960s shows demonstrators participating in a sit-in at a segregated lunch counter in the American South. Civil rights activists — Black and some white — are seated at the counter while onlookers and counter staff are visible. The demonstrators sit calmly and are dressed neatly, practicing the nonviolent direct action strategy taught by civil rights organizations to challenge racial segregation in public accommodations.

(Photograph, c. 1960. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.)

Analyze how the sit-in movement demonstrated the tension between state segregation laws and the constitutional rights guaranteed to all citizens.

choices.text: Sit-ins demonstrated that state segregation laws were constitutional because no federal court had yet overturned them
Sit-ins exposed the conflict between state Jim Crow laws and the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection guarantee, demonstrating the need for federal action to enforce constitutional rights
Sit-ins showed that the Supreme Court's ruling in Brown v. Board of Education was sufficient to end all forms of segregation without additional legislation
Sit-ins primarily highlighted the tension between the First Amendment right to free speech and state criminal trespassing laws

items.explanation: Sit-ins directly exposed the conflict between state-enforced Jim Crow segregation laws — which required separation of races in public accommodations — and the constitutional guarantees of equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. When protesters were arrested for simply sitting at a lunch counter, it highlighted that state laws were being used to deny citizens their constitutional rights, a contradiction that ultimately required federal legislative and judicial action to resolve. The Civil Rights Act of 1964's public accommodations provisions directly addressed this tension. Choice A inverts the constitutional argument. Choice C misidentifies the legal mechanism that resolved the tension. Choice D misattributes the argument — sit-ins addressed civil and constitutional rights, not criminal law.
